How Long Term Stress Affects the Brains of Founders
What long term stress does to your hormones, and how to reduce the response.
How Long Term Stress Affects the Brains of Founders

Stress is not always harmful. A tight deadline can increase focus, a hard negotiation can improve performance, and a near miss can teach faster than a course. The problem for founders is not that stress occurs. The problem is that it often continues for a long time. Managing stress as a founder starts with understanding the system under the feeling. That system is a hormone loop built for short emergencies that is now asked to run for years.
This article explains what that loop does, why founders stay in a stressed state longer than many other people, and three measured ways to reduce it.
The HPA axis, the stress response system in the body

When the brain perceives a threat, it triggers a chain called the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis, or HPA axis. The hypothalamus signals the pituitary gland, which signals the adrenal glands, which release cortisol. Alongside a faster release of adrenaline, cortisol makes energy available, increases attention on the threat and pauses long term processes such as digestion, repair and immune maintenance.

In a healthy system, the same cortisol that rises also turns the response off. Once levels climb high enough, they signal the brain and the axis slows down. The threat passes, the body recovers, and cortisol returns to its normal daily pattern, highest in the morning and lowest around midnight.
Cortisol should peak within an hour of waking and fall to its lowest point around midnight. Chronic stress flattens that curve, leaving you wired at night and drained in the morning.
Why founders stay in a state of stress

The HPA axis responds in the same way to a physical threat and to a payroll problem. It responds to perceived threat, uncertainty and lack of control, and founders live with all three in high amounts.
The threat does not fully end

Most professionals face stressors with a beginning and an end. A project is delivered, or a quarter closes. A founder faces stressors such as cash runway, product market fit and the livelihoods of the team, which stay open for months or years. The stress response is never formally ended.
Personal identity is linked to the company

When the company is struggling, many founders experience it as a judgement of themselves. Stress researchers have identified social evaluative threat, meaning the fear of being judged as failing, as one of the most reliable triggers of a strong cortisol response.
Recovery activities are cut first

The behaviours that reset the system are sleep, movement, time with people who have nothing to do with the business, and real rest time. Those are the activities founders cut when work increases. Stress rises and recovery falls at the same time.
Short term stress compared with long term stress
It helps to separate two very different states that share the same name.
Acute stress

is short and has a clear end. It improves reaction time, memory for the event and motivation. Robert Sapolsky observed that a zebra chased by a lion experiences extreme stress for a few minutes and then, if it survives, returns to grazing. That is the system working as designed.
Chronic stress

is the same response held on for weeks. Over time the feedback loop that should turn the axis off becomes less sensitive. Cortisol stays elevated or its daily pattern flattens. Sleep becomes lighter and more broken. Neuroscience research, including work from Amy Arnsten at Yale, shows that long term stress signalling weakens the prefrontal cortex, the region used for planning and self control, while strengthening the more reactive circuits around the amygdala.
Long term stress shifts control from the prefrontal cortex, which plans, to the amygdala, which reacts. The result is a shorter temper and a focus on shorter time periods.

For a founder, long term stress rarely appears only as anxiety. It can appear as irritability with the team, delaying hard decisions, heavier use of caffeine and alcohol, and a feeling that every week requires maximum effort. We cover how this changes the quality of choices in

Managing stress as a founder, three measured actions

The aim is not to eliminate stress. The aim is to restore the ability to turn the response off, so pressure comes in periods rather than staying constant. Each action below has research behind it and gives you something to measure.
1. Five minutes of cyclic sighing

A 2023 Stanford study published in Cell Reports Medicine compared several five-minute daily breathing practices with mindfulness meditation over a month. Cyclic sighing, a double inhale through the nose followed by a long, slow exhale through the mouth, produced the greatest improvement in mood and the largest drop in resting breathing rate.
Do it between meetings, before a difficult call or in the car before you walk into the house.
Measure it:
note your resting breathing rate or stress rating before and after for two weeks.
2. Exercise regularly at a moderate level

Regular aerobic exercise is one of the most consistent findings in stress research. People who are fitter tend to show a smaller physical reaction to the same psychological stressor, and recover from it faster. Consistency matters more than intensity. Do three to five sessions a week of brisk walking, cycling or running at a pace where you can still talk. Very hard training added to a heavy work week can add to the load rather than relieve it.
Measure it:
track sessions per week and your morning resting heart rate. A rising trend over several days is a reliable sign that you have not recovered enough.
3. End each work day with a set routine

Long term stress increases when work has no clear ending. Give each workday a fixed ending routine. Review the three priorities for tomorrow, write down anything still on your mind, and then close the laptop. The specific routine matters less than doing it every day. It signals to the HPA axis that the work threat has been handled for today.
Measure it:
rate your stress from 1 to 10 at the end of each day for two weeks and watch the trend, not the single days.
Know your numbers

Founders measure many things in the business and few things about their own health. A daily stress rating and a weekly view of sleep will tell you more about your direction than any single bad day.
